label: Claude Fable 5.2
output:
**Last night**

I haven't posted here since spring. Every time I thought about it, the only thing I had to say was about staffing, and I've written enough of those. This is about something else.

On Saturday I did my last ever night shift. Majors, 21:00 to 07:30. As of Monday I'm on the days-only rota. My first night was as an SHO in 2012, so that's fourteen years of them, and I am surprisingly not okay about it.

The reasons for the move are boring. My knees. My sleep, which stopped bouncing back between runs of nights a while ago. And my GP, who told me my blood pressure is not a joke anymore. I'm 42 and I'd assumed I had a few more years before anyone used that tone with me.

I've tried to write this several times since Sunday. Each attempt turned into either a eulogy or a complaint, and I don't want either. Nobody has died, and I asked for this. So I'm going to try to be straight about what nights gave me and what they took.

What they took comes first, because that's the easier list.

My first winter of nights, I cried in the car park at the Infirmary because I couldn't remember whether I'd given a second dose. I had. That's the whole story. Nobody came to harm. But I can still see the frost on the windscreen. Anyone who's worked nights knows that kind of doubt, the one that turns up at the end of a shift when you're too tired to trust your own memory of your own hands. It got rarer over the years, but it never completely went.

They took family things too. My sister lives in Bangalore, and both of my nieces had naming ceremonies that I was meant to join by video. Both times I was on nights, and I missed them. My sister has never once complained. She reads this blog, so I'll say it here: I noticed that you never said anything. I've thought about it a lot.

And they took the things that sent me to the GP. I wouldn't have admitted that a couple of years ago. Nights felt like something I was good at, and it's hard to accept that a thing you're good at has been costing you the whole time.

Now for what they gave me, which is harder to write without going soppy.

Nights are where the department is most itself. There are fewer managers about, and what's left is more honest and, oddly, kinder. People tell you when they're struggling. People tell you when you're wrong. Someone you barely know will take a job off your list without being asked because they can see you're flagging, and an hour later you'll do the same for them.

People think nights are about adrenaline. There's some of that. But mostly it's about staying kind at 5am when you're empty, and that's the thing I'm proudest of having learned, on the nights I managed it. I didn't always.

Last winter, at about three in the morning, an old gentleman held my hand and told me I had his daughter's hands. I'm not going to say anything more about him, except that he went home three days later. I've had plenty of dramatic nights in fourteen years and that's the one I keep coming back to this week. Maybe it could have happened at three in the afternoon. I just don't think I'd have had the time to stand still for it.

On Sunday morning I drove home down the London Road with the sun coming up and the shipping forecast on catch-up. Somewhere along there it landed on me that I won't see that light from this side again. I'll see sunrises, obviously. I'll be driving to work under them. But the one you get at the end of a night, when you're going to bed as everyone else is getting up, that one's done.

So I'm relieved. And I feel like a traitor for being relieved. The people I worked with on Saturday will be back for their next run of nights and I won't. My body is frankly delighted and the rest of me hasn't caught up. I don't have a neat way of resolving that. I think both things are going to be true for a while.

What helps is remembering that nights never depended on me.

Folasade, our charge nurse on nights, has been doing them for 22 years. She still beats me up the stairs, and I stopped pretending I was letting her a long time ago.

And then there's the toast. At 4am, every night, someone makes toast in the staff room. Nobody admits to starting it. I've never got to the bottom of it, and I've come to think it's better that way. You walk in, the room smells of toast, and for a few minutes the night feels manageable.

Tonight at four, someone will put bread in the toaster in that staff room. On the nights she's in, Folasade will be up the stairs ahead of whoever's trying to keep up with her. And at five, somebody running on nothing will be kind to a stranger anyway. All of that carries on, and I'm glad it does.

If you're on tonight and it's you who starts the toast, your secret's safe.

---

That's about 900 words. A few lines are my guesses at how you feel, not things you told me, so change or cut any that aren't true:

- **The GP's tone:** "I'd assumed I had a few more years before anyone used that tone with me."
- **Being good at nights:** the paragraph about it being hard to accept that something you're good at has been costing you.
- **How colleagues behave:** people telling you when you're wrong, and taking jobs off your list.
- **The old gentleman:** the line about not having had time to stand still for it in the afternoon.
- **The toast:** that you've never found out who starts it.

It's also worth checking that Folasade is happy to be named.
